ELF's slide-level architecture is designed for data-efficient downstream evaluation, including settings with limited data such as therapeutic response prediction. We evaluate ELF for disease classification and biomarker detection, as well as anticancer and immunotherapy response prediction across multiple cancer types. ELF achieves higher performance than the evaluated constituent and slide-level foundation models across the tested tasks, supporting further evaluation of ensemble learning for pathology applications in oncology.

title: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: The Vision of Heracles
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains among the deadliest malignancies, as tumors evolve faster than therapies. Resistance is ecological, not merely KRAS driven, involving overlooked players like high-grade pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasias (PanINs), peripancreatic fat, stromal mechanics, myeloid-neural circuits, metabolic rewiring, and systemic host responses. We propose precision interception targeting PanIN/intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) biology, spatial-functional-proteogenomic classification beyond transcriptomics, the Heracles Protocol (measure, prime, strike, and adapt), and integrated technologies from AI pathology to exosomal delivery and CRISPR-based synergy mapping, together making PDAC more tractable.

title: Molecular residual disease: Charting a new path for treating resectable solid tumors
abstract: Molecular residual disease (MRD), detected via circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) after curative-intent surgery, identifies resectable solid tumor patients at high recurrence risk, thereby enabling enriched trials with larger effect sizes and smaller samples. Yet enrichment narrows the eligible population and thus challenges conventional randomized designs. We propose an MRD Registry as an external control cohort that integrates quantitative ctDNA data with outcomes to validate ctDNA dynamics as response indicators-facilitating efficient MRD-based trial design and accelerating novel therapy development.

title: Scherer’s map, remapped
abstract: Scherer's century-old classification of expansive and infiltrative glioma growth remains foundational to neuro-oncology. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Hoefflin et al. use spatial RNA and protein profiling of IDH-mutant gliomas to reveal hypoxia and necrosis as organizing centers of expansive growth and white-matter tracts as guides and constraints on invasion.

title: Spatial analysis reveals the evolving organization of IDH-mutant glioma
abstract: Adult diffuse gliomas are composed of malignant cell states interwoven with the non-malignant brain microenvironment. Here, we combine spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)-mutant gliomas to define organizational principles across histological grades. In low-grade tumors, spatial organization is shaped by underlying brain anatomy. We identify a functional white-gray matter junction that restricts cortical invasion and is associated with marked changes in tumor composition and cellular phenotypes. This junction is preferentially traversed by oligodendrocyte progenitor (OPC)-like malignant cells, suggesting a role in tumor expansion. In contrast, tumors with intermediate histological features are largely disorganized, with few recurring interactions between cancer cell states and microenvironmental cell types. In high-grade tumors, hypoxia-associated structure emerges, resembling IDH-wild-type glioblastoma. Together, these findings reveal two independent axes of spatial organization-from anatomy-driven structure in low-grade tumors to hypoxia-driven organization in high-grade tumors-and establish a framework linking tumor grade to recurrent spatial interactions.

title: Chronotherapy with immune checkpoint inhibitors: The knowns, the unknowns, and the contested
abstract: Emerging data indicate that immune checkpoint inhibitors can exhibit time-of-day-dependent effects in pre-clinical models. Furthermore, multiple retrospective clinical trials associate earlier anti-tumor treatment timing with improved outcomes. However, key questions remain regarding the reproducibility of these findings, the underlying mechanisms, and their clinical implications. This commentary discusses these open questions and provides an outlook on the field.

title: Chemotherapy-free phase 1/2 trial of HRS-4642 plus adebrelimab in previously treated metastatic KRAS G12D-mutant pancreatic cancer
abstract: KRAS G12D mutations drive approximately 40% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) cases and foster an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. This phase 1/2 trial (NCT06427239) evaluated HRS-4642, a selective KRAS G12D inhibitor, combined with the PD-L1 blockade adebrelimab in 48 pretreated patients with metastatic KRAS G12D-mutant PDAC. Dose escalation revealed no dose-limiting toxicities, establishing the recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D), and no treatment-related deaths occurred; hypercholesterolemia and anemia (each 50%) were the most common treatment-related adverse events. In the RP2D cohort (n = 37), the confirmed objective response rate was 43.2% (95% confidence interval [CI], 27.1-60.5), disease control rate was 81.1% (95% CI, 64.8-92.0), median duration of response was 6.9 months (95% CI, 4.8-8.6), median progression-free survival was 5.7 months (95% CI, 4.0-7.5), and median overall survival was 11.5 months (95% CI, 9.2-16.9). This chemotherapy-free regimen is tolerable and shows encouraging antitumor activity in refractory KRAS G12D-mutant PDAC, warranting further investigation.

title: Myeloid reprogramming generates myeloid-derived activating cells to potentiate radiotherapy and suppress metastasis
abstract: Radiation induces immunosuppressive myeloid cells that drive therapeutic resistance and metastasis. We identify TET2 as a radiation-induced regulator of myeloid-derived suppressor cells whose expression correlates with poor outcomes in advanced lung cancer patients receiving radio-immunotherapy. Following radiotherapy, myeloid-specific Tet2 deletion suppresses tumor progression and redirects monocyte differentiation toward antigen-presenting myeloid-derived activating cells (MDACs), which augment antitumor T cell responses; spatiotemporal mapping shows that this fate program initiates rapidly in the bone marrow. Mechanistically, a radiation-responsive p53-TET2 axis decreases m 5 C on chromatin-associated RNAs (caRNAs), enforcing immunosuppressive chromatin compaction and silencing interferon signaling, whereas Tet2 loss restores chromatin accessibility and enhances CD8 + T cell cytotoxicity. Pharmacological TET2 inhibition recapitulates this phenotype and augments radiotherapy and PD-L1 blockade to control primary and metastatic tumors. These findings define MDACs as an immunogenic myeloid subset and establish myeloid reprogramming as a strategy to improve radiotherapy-immunotherapy outcomes.

title: Beyond genes and hotspots: Protein-informed interpretation of cancer mutations
abstract: Interpreting the biological and clinical significance of somatic mutations in cancer genomes remains challenging. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Hyeon et al. identify and map significantly mutated regions to protein domains and structural features, establishing a proteo-genomics framework for interpreting cancer mutations beyond genes and hotspots.

title: γδ T cells BiTE back at small cell lung cancer
abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Ng et al. characterize and leverage cytotoxic γδ T cells in small cell lung cancer to overcome unsuccessful checkpoint blockade immunotherapy. Engaging Vδ2 + cells with a bispecific T cell engager (BiTE) bypasses the challenge of low MHC-I expression and ineffective CD8 + T cells.

title: γδ T cells modulate anti-tumor immunity in small cell lung cancer
abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a highly aggressive neoplasm with limited sensitivity to anti-PD-(L)1 blockade, which is likely caused by the epigenetic silencing of MHC-I. Elucidating MHC-I-independent immune recognition mechanisms is therefore crucial for enhancing treatment responses and improving clinical outcomes in a greater number of patients. Leveraging single-cell approaches, we discovered γδ T cell infiltration in biospecimens from patients with SCLC. Despite PD-1 expression, γδ T cells maintained a cytotoxic transcriptional profile, suggesting an anti-tumor role. Indeed, high γδ T cell infiltration in two practice-changing clinical trials predicted improved response to anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy in patients with SCLC. Moreover, using preclinical models, we demonstrated that γδ T cells are effective at tarlatamab (delta-like ligand 3 [DLL3]-CD3 bispecific T cell engager [BiTE])-redirected SCLC killing and that zoledronate, an FDA-approved compound, can sensitize SCLC cells to γδ T cell-mediated killing. Thus, our findings suggest that engaged γδ T cells are potentially valuable targets for SCLC therapy.

title: Human-centric preclinical models for CAR T cell therapy in solid tumors: Where patient-derived organoids fit
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has shown promising activity in solid tumors, yet translational progress remains limited by preclinical models that incompletely capture human tumor biology. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) preserve key features of human tumors, including cellular heterogeneity and tissue architecture, thereby enabling functional evaluation of CAR T cell targets, next-generation approaches, resistance mechanisms, and selected safety considerations. We discuss how PDOs complement existing preclinical platforms to support CAR T cell development for solid tumors.

title: The wu wei of brain metastases: When the gift of a pause is also a vulnerability
abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, García-Gómez et al. show that brain-seeding cancer cells exploit an MXD4-dependent proliferative pause that enables survival under stress before metastatic outgrowth. By restraining MYC and activating protective stress responses, this pause becomes an Achilles' heel, potentially targetable to eradicate micrometastases before clinical relapse.

title: A transient MXD4-dependent proliferative pause enables survival of brain micrometastases
abstract: Successful metastatic colonization requires cancer cells to survive multiple stresses during early organ adaptation, yet how metastasis-initiating cells overcome this bottleneck remains unknown. Here, we identify a transient MXD4-dependent proliferative pause that enables aggressive cancer cells to survive early brain colonization. Before vascular co-option-associated outgrowth, metastatic cells temporarily restrain proliferation through the MYC antagonist MXD4, buffering stresses encountered after extravasation. Genetic disruption of MXD4 compromises survival of micrometastases, preventing their progression to macrometastases. Analyses of human brain micrometastases validate this transient adaptive state in patients. Exploiting vulnerabilities associated with the proliferative pause reveals preventive therapeutic opportunities across experimental settings, including spontaneous brain metastasis models and minimal residual disease following neurosurgical resection. In addition, patient-derived organotypic cultures confirm the feasibility of targeting this state with clinically available drugs. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized adaptive stage during metastatic colonization and identify actionable vulnerabilities to prevent brain metastasis progression and relapse.

title: Beyond BMI: The diet-microbiome context of the obesity paradox
abstract: In Nature, Desharnais et al. show that in diverse mouse models, anti-PD-1 sensitivity is more closely linked to the diet-microbiome-metabolite ecosystem than to obesity-associated metabolic dysfunction. Their findings reinforce body mass index (BMI) as an incomplete proxy for host biology and suggest strategies to improve anti-PD-1 efficacy without inducing obesity.

title: Chemotherapy enhances cancer vaccine efficacy and expands stem-like TCF1+CD8+ T cells
abstract: Summary Therapeutic cancer vaccines, whether based on neoantigens or shared antigens, will likely be given in the clinic together with the standard of care, which often comprises immune checkpoint blockade therapy and chemotherapy. It remains unclear, however, whether vaccines effectively synergize with chemotherapy. Here, we tested the combination of a heterologous prime-boost viral vector vaccine with chemotherapy (CarboTaxol) and anti-PD- 1. We show that this triple combination improves tumor control and survival in different murine tumor models. CarboTaxol, and also cyclophosphamide, acted as an immune adjuvant for the vaccines, enhancing tumor-specific CD8+ T-cell responses, irrespective of the presence of a tumor. These chemotherapies expanded stem-like T cell factor 1 (TCF1)+CD8+ T cells. Inhibition of the transcriptional activity of TCF1/β-catenin with a small molecule inhibitor abolished the immune adjuvant effect of CarboTaxol. This study sheds light on the new immunomodulatory roles of chemotherapies and holds promises for clinical testing of this combination strategy. Highlights The combination of CarboTaxol with viral vector cancer vaccines and anti-PD-1 promotes better tumor control, tumor clearance, and survival CarboTaxol increases TCF1 expression in CD8+ T cells and expands stem-like TCF1+CD8+ T cells CarboTaxol acts as an adjuvant for cancer vaccines irrespective of the presence of a tumor and this effect is mediated by TCF1/β-catenin activity

title: Chromatin accessibility trajectories reveal pre-cancerous epigenetic priming and an acid-driven immunotherapy-resistant gastric cancer subtype
abstract: Chromatin remodeling is prominent in cancers, yet it remains obscure how chromatin dynamics underlies stepwise tumorigenesis and informs anti-cancer therapeutics. By decoding a large-scale chromatin accessibility atlas of 650 multistage samples from 439 patients, we delineate epigenetic switches spanning multistep gastric tumorigenesis. A cancer-resembling epigenetic priming state in intestinal metaplasia licenses subsequent tumor initiation. In advanced malignancies, inter-tumoral diversity stratifies three epigenomic subtypes. The proliferative and mesenchymal-inflammatory subtypes are sensitive to neoadjuvant immunotherapy, while the pseudo-gastric subtype is intrinsically drug resistant. Mechanistically, the refractory subtype is featured by a unique gastric lineage-mimicking phenotype, governed in part by FOSL2 to up-regulate H + /K + ATPase transporters and sculpt an acidic milieu suppressing CD8 + T cells. Inhibition of this phenotype by either FOSL2 depletion or vonoprazan, a clinically available acid blocker, sensitizes immunotherapy. Collectively, these findings highlight that chromatin accessibility dynamics facilitates sequential tumorigenesis from gastric pre-cancer and defines subtypes exploitable to guide immunotherapy and overcome drug resistance.

title: Chromatin plasticity and lineage repurposing: When gastric identity turns acidic
abstract: Chromatin dynamics shape gastric cancer at every stage. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Wang et al. uncover a premalignant chromatin state primed for oncogenic activation alongside a pseudo-gastric subtype that hijacks acid secretion to evade antitumor immunity, revealing gastric proton pumps as a potential therapeutic target.

title: Spatial omics resolves adrenergic and mesenchymal cell states in neuroblastoma
abstract: Neuroblastoma is a pediatric cancer arising from the developing sympathoadrenal lineage. Although cell lines derived from neuroblastoma patients have features of either adrenergic (ADRN) or mesenchymal (MES) cells, identifying MES cells in patient tumors is challenging and controversial. Here, to characterize intra- and inter-patient cellular heterogeneity, we analyze 54 neuroblastoma tumors spanning broad clinical, genetic, and histologic features using single-cell/single-nucleus RNA sequencing (sc/snRNA-seq), bulk RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and spatial proteomics. We show that tumor cells occupy distinct cellular neighborhoods separated from nonmalignant immune and stromal cells, yet established cell line-derived gene expression signatures fail to identify MES neuroblastoma cells. We therefore develop ADRN/MES signatures from early-passage orthotopic patient-derived xenografts, enabling the identification of MES tumor cells, validated by transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, ultrastructural, and functional assays. In patients, high MES gene expression correlates with worse event-free and overall survival. Together, this study provides a framework for defining clinically relevant neuroblastoma cell states.

title: Microbial cues for a stem-like lymphoid niche
abstract: While tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) broadly correlate with immunotherapy efficacy, their functional heterogeneity can translate into divergent clinical outcomes. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Hu et al. uncover a microbiota-orchestrated stem-like lymphoid niche in which CD70 + ILC2s sustain progenitor exhausted T cells, and their findings redefine the functional organization underlying TLS-associated antitumor immunity.

title: Toward the next generation of CAR T cell therapies for cancer
abstract: With seven products approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for 15 indications and more than 2,600 active clinical trials, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy is firmly established as an effective therapeutic modality for cancer treatment, and promising early data demonstrate its potential in autoimmune diseases. Key challenges facing the field include extending efficacy to solid tumors and reducing the cost and complexity of manufacturing to improve patient access. In this review, we summarize the clinical lessons learned from the now substantial experience with commercial CAR T cells and clinical trials and discuss three waves shaping next-generation development: multi-engineered and logic-gated CAR T cells, rational combination strategies, and in vivo CAR T cell generation. By integrating clinical experience with emerging strategies, we highlight where CAR T cell therapy has succeeded, where current approaches remain insufficient, and how next-generation cell therapies may be designed to overcome these barriers.

title: Hitting KRAS G12D without the gut punch: Can immunotherapy make it last?
abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Shi et al. report encouraging early-phase results combining HRS-4642, an allele-specific KRAS G12D inhibitor, with the PD-L1 inhibitor adebrelimab in previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer. The intravenous combination was safe and well tolerated, notably sparing patients the gastrointestinal toxicity common to oral KRAS inhibitors, and achieved a promising 43% response rate at the recommended dose.

title: One structural class, one treatment? Firmonertinib in PACC-mutant NSCLC
abstract: EGFR PACC-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) has limited treatment options. In this issue of Cancer Cell, Le et al. report preclinical profiles and promising systemic and intracranial efficacy of the broad-spectrum CNS-penetrant tyrosine kinase inhibitor firmonertinib in PACC-mutant NSCLC, supporting its further clinical development in this challenging mutation class.

title: Firmonertinib in advanced non-small cell lung cancer with epidermal growth factor receptor P-loop and αC-helix compressing mutations
abstract: P-loop and αC-helix compressing (PACC) mutations comprise a structurally distinct subgroup of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with limited treatment options. Firmonertinib is a once-daily oral, brain-penetrant, mutant-selective EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor with a unique trifluoroethoxy side chain. Firmonertinib had high anti-proliferative efficacy in EGFR PACC-mutant cells and xenografts. In the phase 1b FURTHER study (NCT05364073), patients with metastatic EGFR PACC-mutant NSCLC randomized to receive first-line firmonertinib 160 mg (n = 25) or 240 mg (n = 22) had confirmed objective response rates (ORRs) of 43% and 68%, median duration of response not reached and 14.6 months, and median progression-free survival of 11.1 and 16.0 months, respectively; treatment-related adverse events led to dose reductions (19% and 24%) and discontinuation (3% and 0%). Intracranial ORR among patients with brain metastases at baseline was 47% (8/17). Results support further study of first-line firmonertinib in patients with EGFR PACC-mutant NSCLC.

title: Mechanisms of Progression of Myeloid Preleukemia to Transformed Myeloid Leukemia in Children with Down Syndrome
Lung neuroendocrine cancer induces immunosuppressive macrophages via serotonin to drive resistance to the T cell engager tarlatamab
abstract: Tarlatamab, a delta-like protein 3 (DLL3) × CD3-directed T cell engager (TCE), provides clinical efficacy against small cell lung cancers (SCLCs), although its efficacy remains limited, indicating the importance of clarifying the resistance mechanisms. We show that serotonin (5-HT) produced by DLL3 high neuroendocrine cancers (NECs) induces immunosuppressive tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), resulting in impaired CD8 + T cell function and TCE resistance. Using SCLC and large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma cohorts, we find that DLL3 high SCLCs induce immunosuppressive TAMs in the tumor microenvironment and become resistant to tarlatamab. DLL3 high NECs increase 5-HT production via TPH1 upregulation. NEC-derived 5-HT augments the immunosuppressive activity of 5-HT receptor 7 (HTR7)-expressing TAMs. Genetic ablation of HTR7 in TAMs or TPH1 in NECs restores CD8 + T cell function and improves the efficacy of TCEs and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockade. We propose that NEC-derived 5-HT-HTR7 axis drives immunosuppressive TAM activation and TCE resistance, making it a key target to increase TCE efficacy.

title: Multiomic characterization of microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer reveals distinct biology and targetable vulnerabilities
abstract: Microsatellite-stable (MSS) colorectal cancer (CRC) is a molecularly complex and clinically challenging disease subtype, lacking effective targeted therapies. Leveraging multiomic data from ∼2,000 tumor samples (including 316MSS CRCs not previously profiled) representing ∼4,500 molecular profiles and 195,246 single cells/nuclei, we uncover complex biology and therapeutic vulnerabilities. Application of a multiomic-phenomic integrative framework, including iPhenMap (a machine-learning tool), reveals complex molecular programs, including replication stress, right-sided biology, glutaminolysis-driven metabolic reprogramming, and MYC-E2F transcriptional networks governing epigenetic remodeling and perineural invasion. Focusing on RAS-mutant MSS CRC, functional validation in state-of-the-art patient-derived tumoroid and matched xenograft models confirms focal adhesion kinase (FAK), phosphoinositide-dependent kinase (PDK)1/2, and proteasome inhibition as potential therapeutic strategies when combined with mitogen-activated protein kinase (MEK) blockade. This work underscores the power of integrated multiomic profiling and functional modeling to refine potential treatment approaches in MSS CRC patient populations.

title: How far are we from multi-omics states to therapeutic targets in microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer?
abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Sadanandam et al. integrate multi-omics profiling of microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer with patient-derived models, identifying focal adhesion kinase and phosphoinositide-dependent kinase 1 as promising therapeutic targets. The study advances multi-omics discoveries toward functional precision oncology and potential treatment strategies to guide clinical translation.

title: The neoantigen quality model: Is closer to self more non-self?
abstract: T cells recognize antigens from pathogens and transformed cells. Yet what antigen is "ideal"? We propose a theoretical framework in which recognition is governed by T cell selection maximized near, not far from, self. Genomic errors generate antigens closer to self that paradoxically overlap with pathogen antigens and are immunogenic and non-self. We formalize this concept as the Neoantigen Quality Model, recasting antigen recognition as an adaptation to surveil the self and non-self living worlds.

title: Finding MES: A hidden cell state in neuroblastoma
abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Patel et al. integrate bulk and single-cell/single-nucleus RNA sequencing with spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics across neuroblastoma patient-derived xenografts and annotated tumors to reveal adrenergic and mesenchymal signatures, identify distinct tumor cell populations in vivo, and demonstrate associations with patient outcomes.

title: Macrophage lipid signaling drives glioblastoma invasion and represents a therapeutic vulnerability
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by diffuse infiltration into the surrounding brain, limiting complete surgical resection, the strongest determinant of patient survival. The mechanisms driving this invasive growth remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify a lipid-mediated paracrine signaling axis through which tumor-associated microglia/macrophages promote glioma invasion. Integrating single-cell transcriptomics, spatial lipidomics, and functional perturbation across mouse models and human GBM samples, we show that invading tumor cells engage and reprogram myeloid cells via colony-stimulating factor-1 receptor (CSF1R)-PI3K signaling. This induces lipid metabolic reprogramming and secretion of bioactive lipids, including lysophosphatidylcholines (LPCs) and lysophosphatidic acids (LPAs), which promote GBM invasion through distinct downstream pathways. Disruption of this myeloid-GBM axis reduces lipid secretion and suppresses invasion. Targeting downstream LPA-LPA receptor (LPAR) or YAP/TAZ signaling further constrains invasion in a context-dependent manner. Together, these findings define a lipid-driven circuit linking the tumor microenvironment to glioma invasion and identify strategies to reduce infiltration and improve surgical resection.

title: CPS + EG and Neo-Bioscore predict individual outcomes but not trial results after neoadjuvant therapy for early breast cancer
abstract: CPS + EG and Neo-Bioscore are prognostic scores estimating the risk of recurrence after neoadjuvant chemotherapy for early breast cancer, but can they predict the long-term outcomes in a clinical trial? In this study, we assessed their surrogacy values at patient level and trial level for long-term outcomes, using data from 8,359 patients across nine neoadjuvant randomized trials conducted by the German Breast Group (GBG) and AGO-B study group. We found that at the patient level, both scores were significantly associated with outcomes, but at the trial level, the associations with distant disease-free survival (DDFS), invasive disease-free survival (iDFS), and overall survival (OS) were weak for both scores (R 2 range = 0.03 to 0.24, with wide confidence intervals). Thus, our findings suggest that CPS + EG and Neo-Bioscore are not reliable surrogate endpoints for predicting long-term treatment benefit in neoadjuvant trials but remain valuable for estimating individual patients' residual risk after neoadjuvant treatments and guiding subsequent treatment decisions for early breast cancer patients.

title: Antibiotics and outcomes of cancer immunotherapy: An updated meta-analysis and clinical applications
abstract: The gut microbiome is a modifiable determinant of response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI), positioning antibiotic exposure as a critical yet under-recognized risk factor for worse survival outcomes in immuno-oncology. As nearly 30% of ICI-treated patients receive antibiotics and indications of cancer immunotherapy are expanding, this issue represents a global challenge in oncology. Here, we paint an updated and comprehensive landscape of antibiotic exposure in immuno-oncology, provide actionable clinical recommendations, and envision future avenues for improvement. First, we describe the biological mechanisms by which antibiotic-induced dysbiosis contributes to ICI resistance. Next, through an updated meta-analysis of 116 cohorts and 97,850 cancer patients treated with ICI, we found a significant association between antibiotic exposure and survival outcomes (overall survival, hazard ratio [HR]: 1.49, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.34-1.65; progression-free survival, HR: 1.44, 95% CI: 1.31-1.58). Finally, we discuss antibiotics stewardship and microbiome-centered strategies to prevent, diagnose, and/or repair dysbiosis.

title: KRASG12D-targeted therapy sensitivity depends on interferon signaling activation in pancreatic cancer
abstract: KRAS G12D is a predominant driver in pancreatic cancer, yet the basis of intrinsic resistance to KRAS G12D -targeted therapy remains poorly defined. Integrated genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics profiling across 242 patient-derived organoids (PDOs) and matched tumor tissues reveals a KRAS G12D -mutant subset intrinsically resistant to KRAS G12D -targeted therapeutics, characterized by marked downregulation of innate immune signaling pathways. Functional validation demonstrates that suppressing interferon signaling in sensitive models induces resistance, whereas activation of interferon signaling, particularly interferon beta (IFN-β), increases sensitivity in resistant models. Combining IFN-β with KRAS inhibitors (MRTX1133, HRS-4642, and RMC-6236) exhibits synergistic antitumor effects in intrinsically resistant pancreatic cancer. Mechanistically, sustained MYC activity is associated with attenuated sensitivity to KRAS inhibition and correlates with repressed interferon signaling, suggesting a potential role in promoting intrinsic resistance. These findings identify interferon signaling as a candidate determinant of KRAS-targeted therapy response and support interferon-based combinations as a potential strategy for intrinsically resistant pancreatic cancer.

title: Intrinsic resistance to KRAS inhibition: Interfering with interferon
abstract: In this issue of Cancer Cell, Zhang et al. perform multi-omics profiling on a large collection of patient-derived pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma organoids to elucidate the mechanisms underlying intrinsic resistance to KRAS inhibition. This work identifies suppression of innate immune signaling through sustained MYC activity as the principal driver of intrinsic resistance.

title: A sex-specific platelet switch controls anti-tumor immunity in glioblastoma
abstract: Sex differences in cancer outcome, including that of glioblastoma (GBM), are shaped by biological, hormonal, and immunological factors and impact disease progression, treatment responses, survival, and tumor microenvironment (TME) interactions. Platelets regulate the immune responses and tumor progression in many cancers, but it is not clear how they contribute to these sex-based differences by affecting the dynamics of the TME. Here, we show that GBM patients exhibit heightened platelet reactivity driven by PAR4 signaling. In murine GBM models, both pharmacological inhibition of PAR4 using BMS986120 and genetic deletion of PAR4 significantly prolong survival in females but not males. This survival advantage is estrogen dependent: it is preserved in chromosomal male-hormonal female mice within the four-core genotype model and is rescued in ovariectomized mice treated with estrogen. The survival benefit is TME specific and is mediated by platelet-driven enhancement of CD8⁺ T cell infiltration into the tumor. Inhibition of platelet PAR4 signaling increases calcium signaling through an estrogen-dependent interaction between PAR4 and estrogen receptor β (ERβ)-a receptor interaction not previously described. PAR4-activated platelets within the TME suppress CD8⁺ T cell function, and depletion of CD8⁺ T cells abolishes both the tumor-induced platelet reactivity and the survival benefit conferred by PAR4 inhibition. These findings establish platelet-mediated PAR4 signaling as a critical driver of tumor progression and identify sex-specific immune responses as key to therapeutic efficacy.
